Superheat — evaporator outlet

Uses the dew-point saturation temperature for blends, single saturation temp for pure refrigerants.

Superheat
—

Typical targets: TXV systems 8–12 °F at the evaporator outlet under load; flooded / recirculated ammonia systems run near 0–2 °F by design — don't chase TXV numbers on a flooded coil. Always confirm against the equipment maker's spec.

Subcooling — liquid line

Uses the bubble-point saturation temperature for blends.

Subcooling
—

Typical targets: 5–15 °F on TXV / DX systems. Near-zero subcooling with a hunting TXV points to flash gas or low charge; very high subcooling can mean overcharge or a restriction stacking liquid in the condenser.

How to measure it right

  • Clamp the probe where the bulb sits — same spot on the suction line, insulated over the probe, on a clean horizontal run.
  • Take pressure at the same point — suction pressure at the evaporator outlet, not at the compressor, or line drop will fake extra superheat.
  • Let it settle — wait for steady load and stable pressures before trusting a number; a swinging TXV needs 10–15 minutes.
  • Ammonia note: most industrial R-717 systems are flooded or liquid-overfeed — superheat there is a diagnostic, not a charging target.

Troubleshooter

Pick the symptom you're seeing. Each one lists the most likely causes first and what to check, in the order an experienced tech would work through them. Written for ammonia and general refrigeration plant work.

Coil Checker — is that solenoid energized?

An energized solenoid coil makes a magnetic field. Your phone has a magnetometer (the sensor behind the compass) — this checker is already running the whole time you're on this tab, no button to start it. Just hold the phone against the coil and it reads the field live. A clear jump over the background field means the coil is powered.

  1. Set your baseline first. Tap Set baseline while holding the phone a foot or more away from any coil, motor, or steel. That records the normal background field where you're standing.
  2. Press the back of the phone flat against the coil — right on the coil cap / center nut of the solenoid valve. The magnetometer sits near the top-back of most phones, so try the top edge if the reading doesn't move.
  3. Read the verdict. A strong rise over baseline = ENERGIZED. No change = coil not powered (or open). A weak rise = move closer, re-seat the phone, or the field is being shielded.
  4. Prove it both ways. Have someone cycle the valve or watch the reading drop when the call for the valve ends. A reading that follows the call is a reading you can trust.
Listening… hold the phone on the coil and watch it spin
Listening…
Hold the phone away from the coil and set your baseline, then press it to the coil.

This device or browser isn't sharing a magnetometer.
That's common — iPhone Safari and many in-app browsers don't expose the magnetic field sensor to web pages, even though the phone has one. Try opening this page in Chrome on Android, where the sensor is normally available. On iPhone, the fallback check still works the old way: listen for the coil's hum / click, feel for the slight pull on a screwdriver tip held to the coil nut, and confirm voltage at the coil terminals with a meter.
⚠ A magnetic reading is a screening test, not proof. A coil can show a field and still have a stuck plunger, and a dead reading doesn't prove the circuit is safe to touch. Before opening anything up, verify with a meter and follow your plant's lockout/tagout procedure.

If the coil reads dead

  • No field + no voltage at terminals — work upstream: control power, fuse, relay / PLC output, thermostat or pressure control not calling.
  • Voltage present + no field — coil is open. Kill power and ohm it out; compare with the coil's rated resistance.
  • Field present + valve won't open — mechanical: stuck plunger, dirt under the seat, wrong coil voltage, or the valve is piped backwards.
  • Field present + coil hot and buzzing — plunger not seating (dirt, bent armature tube) or low voltage. A coil held in that state cooks itself.

Daily rounds — engine room

What to look at, listen to, and log every shift. Adjust pressures and levels to your plant's own operating envelope — this is the walk, not the limits sheet.

Compressors

  • Suction & discharge pressure and temperature — log both; compare with yesterday, not just the limit.
  • Oil level, oil pressure, oil temperature — and look at the oil, not just the sight glass level.
  • Unusual noise or vibration — walk past slow; a change in sound is usually the first failure notice you get.
  • Shaft seal area — sniff and look for oil traces; small leaks grow.

Vessels & evaporators

  • Receiver and surge drum levels — in the normal band, and the level controls actually moving.
  • Evaporator frost pattern — even frost is healthy; a bare patch or a frosted suction line back to the compressor is not.
  • Defrost cycles — confirm they ran, terminated, and the coil drained.

Condensers & safety

  • Head pressure vs. wet-bulb — creeping head pressure means fouling, non-condensables, or a fan/pump problem.
  • Purgers and air vents — non-condensables cost you capacity every hour they sit there.
  • Ammonia detectors reading normal, ventilation fans free to run, eyewash / shower access clear.
  • Relief valves — no isolation valve shut under a relief, no frost or corrosion hiding a weep.
  • Log it all — a round that isn't written down didn't happen when something fails at 2 a.m.

TXV Superheat Tuner

A walk-through, one step at a time. Have your gauges and a clamp probe on the suction line at the bulb before you start.

Step 1 of 6
Rules that don't bend: adjust in small increments (about a quarter to a half turn of the stem at a time), wait a full 10–15 minutes after every adjustment, and never tune a valve on a system that isn't at steady, near-full load. If superheat won't respond, the problem usually isn't the adjustment — check bulb contact, charge, and restrictions first.

Receiver Fill Calculator

The rule: a receiver must never be more than 90% full of liquid — it needs vapor space for thermal expansion, and a liquid-full vessel can hydrostatically rupture when it warms up. Enter the vessel and what the sight glass shows.

Receiver fill
—

Warm-up warning: liquid expands as it warms. A receiver at 85% on a cool morning can pass 90% — or go liquid-full — on a hot afternoon or after pump-down into a warm room. Check the fill at the highest temperature the vessel can reach, not just today's. Volumes here are for the straight shell only; heads add a little extra — another reason to leave margin below 90%.

Leak Response — Ammonia

Work through it in order. This is the general sequence — your plant's emergency action plan and your alarm levels govern; where they differ, the plant plan wins.

Step 1 of 8
  • Know your numbers before you need them: ammonia IDLH is 300 ppm; the smell fades (olfactory fatigue) and is not a safe gauge — detectors and meters are.
  • Only trained, SCBA-equipped responders enter a contaminated area. Nobody goes in alone, and nobody goes in to "just close one valve" without air.
  • Write your plant's numbers on paper in the engine room: emergency coordinator, plant manager, local fire / hazmat, and the ammonia supplier's emergency line — this app can't know them for you.

Floating Head Pressure — Savings

Letting condensing pressure float down with cool weather instead of holding it artificially high is free capacity and free energy. Rule of thumb used here: about 1–1.5% compressor energy saved per 1 °F of condensing temperature drop — adjust it to your machines if you have better data.

Estimated saving
—

Watch the floor: don't float below what your TXVs, oil return, and defrost need — most plants hold a minimum condensing pressure for expansion-valve capacity and hot-gas defrost. The saving is real only down to that floor.

Shift Log / Handover

Fill it in on rounds, then copy it or download it and hand it to the next operator. Nothing is saved in the app — once you leave this screen, it's gone, so hand it over first.

Hand Expansion Valve — Overfeed Systems

For ammonia liquid overfeed (recirculated) systems: a pump feeds more liquid to the evaporator than boils off, and the hand expansion valve is how you set that feed by hand. Adjusting it blind is how coils starve or compressors eat liquid. This tool makes you measure first, check every reading against its safe range, and only then touch the valve.

The ranges below are built from your refrigerant's own P–T table in this app and the target evaporating temperature you picked. They're typical overfeed starting points — your plant's operating procedures and the valve maker's sheet always win.

Step by step — where to measure, what to measure

  1. Look at the surge drum (recirculator) level first. Read the sight glass on the vessel that feeds your evaporator. No level, no adjustment — a valve can't fix an empty drum.
  2. Suction pressure — at the evaporator outlet or the surge drum. Use the gauge or transducer on the vessel / suction header, not at the compressor — line drop lies to you. Enter it below; the tool turns it into a saturation temperature for your refrigerant.
  3. Suction temperature — clamp a probe on the suction line right where it leaves the evaporator (or at the drum outlet), on clean bare pipe, insulated over the probe. A loose probe reads room air, not pipe.
  4. Superheat — read it off your instruments if they show it, or work it out: suction line temperature minus the saturation temperature from step 2. Enter what you have; the tool cross-checks it against your pressure and temperature.
  5. Check every light below. All green = good to adjust. Any yellow = small moves only, then re-measure. Any red = stop. Do not adjust the valve and do not leave the system running on that reading — fix the red first.
  6. Adjust in quarter-turns, then wait. Opening (counterclockwise) feeds more liquid; closing (clockwise) feeds less. One quarter-turn, then wait a full 15–20 minutes and take all four readings again before you touch it again.

Your readings — checked live

1 · Suction pressureNo reading

Where: gauge / transducer at the evaporator outlet or surge drum. What: the pressure of the boiling ammonia in the coil.

2 · Suction temperatureNo reading

Where: clamp probe on the suction line leaving the evaporator, insulated. What: the actual temperature of the vapor (and any liquid) coming back.

3 · Surge drum liquid levelNo reading

Where: the sight glass on the surge drum / recirculator. What: how much liquid the pump has to work with, as a % of the glass.

4 · SuperheatNo reading

Where: from your controls, or suction temperature minus saturation temperature. What: how dry the vapor coming back is. On overfeed, low superheat is normal — zero is not.

Go / No-Go
Enter your readings
All four readings get checked against the ranges for your refrigerant and system.

The ranges this tool checks against

Shown live for the refrigerant and system you picked above — so you can see the validation, not just the verdict.

ReadingGreen — good to goYellow — caution / adjustRed — stop / do not run
Suction pressure———
Suction temperature———
Surge drum level30–60% of the glass20–29% or 61–75%Under 20% (pump starves / cavitates) or over 75% (liquid carryover to the compressor)
Superheat4–12 °F2–4 °F or 12–18 °FUnder 2 °F (liquid floodback risk) or over 18 °F (coil starved)

Why these bands: overfeed evaporators are fed 2–4× the liquid that boils off, so the return is wet by design and superheat runs low — but it must never reach zero at the compressor, and the drum must keep the pump fed without carrying liquid over. Suction pressure bands come straight off your refrigerant's saturation table at the target evaporating temperature (±3 °F green, ±7 °F yellow).

⚠ Ammonia rules don't bend: if a reading is red, the move is to make the system safe and call it in — not to keep tweaking the valve. Never adjust a hand valve on a system you haven't walked first, and never use valve position to mask a low charge, a failed pump, or a level control problem.

Valve Positions — by Manufacturer

Tap a maker to open the valves you'll actually find from them in an ammonia plant, with the position each one belongs in for normal operation, pump-down, defrost, and shutdown. Written in our own words, by valve function — model lines change, functions don't.

Read this first: this is a general field reference, not your plant's procedure. Your P&ID, your written operating procedures, and the valve maker's manual govern. One rule never changes: relief valve isolation (block) valves stay OPEN and locked / car-sealed open in every state — normal, pump-down, defrost, and shutdown. A closed block valve under a relief valve takes that vessel's protection away.

The four states, in plain language

  • Normal operation — the system is making cold: feeds open or controlling, suction and discharge stops open, regulators controlling.
  • Pump-down — you're pulling refrigerant out of a section into the receiver / low side: liquid feed to that section shut, compressor keeps pulling until suction is down, then suction stop shut.
  • Defrost — hot gas is in the coil: liquid feed and suction stop shut, hot-gas solenoid open, suction regulator / defrost relief path set so melt pressure can't over-pressurize the coil.
  • Shutdown — the section or machine is out of service: stops shut, coil isolated, and anything that can trap liquid between two closed valves gets relieved or drained — trapped liquid warming up is a hydrostatic rupture waiting to happen.

  6. 6Liquid NH3 swelling effect is 20% of its original size under standard atmospheric temperatures
  7. 7Liquid NH3 expansion rate at standard atmospheric pressure is 768:1
  8. 8H2O absorption rate of NH3 gas is 1,300:1
  9. 92.5 gallons of water to dilute one pound of ammonia gas
  10. 10pH of NH3 is about 11.6
  11. 11Oils can absorb approximately 1% of ammonia gas by volume
  12. 121 mA is 1/1,000 of an amp
  13. 131 HP = 2,545 BTU's of energy
  14. 14H2O latent heat of boiling is approximately 970 BTU's
  15. 15H2O latent heat of freezing is approximately 144 BTU's
  16. 16°C = {(°F − 32) / 1.8}
  17. 17°F = {(°C × 1.8) + 32}
  18. 18Sensible Heat Equation: BTU's = {Mass × Specific Heat × (T1 − T2)}
  19. 19Latent Heat Equation: BTU's = (Mass × Latent Heat of Freezing)
  20. 20Specific Heat (Cp) of liquid H2O is 1.0
  21. 21Specific Heat (Cp) of liquid NH3 is 1.12
  22. 22Pressure = (Force / Area)
  23. 23PSIA = {14.7 − ("Hg / 2.035)}
  24. 24PSIA = (14.7 + PSIG)
  25. 25PSIG = (PSIA − 14.7)

Formula Calculators

The same formulas with the math done for you. Pressures for ratios are absolute — the calculators add the 14.7 for you.

Compression ratio

Ratio = (Discharge PSIG + 14.7) / (Suction PSIG + 14.7)
—

Single-stage ammonia machines generally live under about 8:1 to 10:1. Ratios climbing past that are why low-temp plants go two-stage — discharge temperature is what pays for a high ratio.

Flash / tax gas % — ammonia

Flash % = {(TD × 1.12) / 561} × 100
—

TD = liquid temp − evaporating temp. That percentage of every pound you feed flashes to gas just cooling the rest down — it does no cooling in the coil, and your valves, lines, and vessel have to carry it.

Sensible heat

BTU's = Mass (lb) × Specific Heat (Cp) × (T1 − T2)
—

Tons of refrigeration

1 ton = 12,000 BTU/hr = 200 BTU/min ≈ 3.517 kW
—

Gauge ↔ absolute pressure

PSIA = 14.7 + PSIG · PSIG = PSIA − 14.7
Type in either box — the other pressure is what ratios and saturation math actually use.

Charts / Graphs

Drawn live from the same CoolProp saturation data as the P–T Slider — pick a refrigerant and see its whole pressure–temperature curve, then compare the common refrigerants side by side.

Saturation curve — pressure vs temperature

The curve is why small temperature changes matter: pressure climbs faster and faster as temperature rises. On ammonia, that curve is the difference between a normal summer head pressure and a relief valve lifting.

Saturation pressure at −20 °F (psig)

Saturation pressure at 100 °F (psig)

Same temperature, wildly different pressures — that's why gauges, hoses, and relief settings are refrigerant-specific, and why CO₂ numbers live in another world from ammonia's.

How to read a P–T chart on a call

  • Pressure first, temperature second. Read the gauge, find that pressure on the chart, and the temperature beside it is what the refrigerant is boiling or condensing at — right now, in that part of the system.
  • Compare it to the metal temperature. Gauge temperature vs. pipe temperature is superheat or subcooling — the two numbers that tell you what the refrigerant is actually doing.
  • Blends have two temperatures. Bubble for liquid, dew for vapor — the Charts above use the dew point for blends, same as the P–T Slider.

Animations

Our own animated diagrams — tap play and watch the refrigerant move. Each one comes with the plain-language version of what's happening.

1 · Basic Refrigeration Cycle

Follow a dot around: the evaporator boils cold liquid and soaks up heat from the room. The compressor squeezes that vapor, making it hot and high-pressure. The condenser dumps the heat outside and the vapor turns back to liquid. The expansion valve drops the pressure, the liquid gets cold again — and part of it flashes to gas on the way through (that's the flash gas from the Formulas tab).

2 · Evaporative Condenser

Hot discharge gas runs through the coil while water rains over it and the fan pulls air up through. The water that evaporates carries the heat away — that's why these condensers follow the wet-bulb temperature, not the air temperature, and why they condense colder than an air-cooled unit on the same day. Scale on that coil is insulation: keep the water treated and the sprays clear.

3 · Plate Heat Exchanger

Two fluids trade heat through thin metal plates without ever touching. Fluid 1 snakes down through every other channel while Fluid 2 snakes up through the channels in between — counter-flow, so the coldest Fluid 2 meets the coldest Fluid 1 and the temperatures can get very close. In ammonia plants these chill water or glycol, condense, or subcool liquid in a footprint a shell-and-tube can't match.

Ask Frosty

Plain answers to ammonia questions, straight from the channel's training library — the PSM book, the Operator's Handbook, and the Deep Dive lessons. Give Frosty real readings — a pressure, a temperature, and the refrigerant — and he'll do the P–T, superheat, subcooling, and compression-ratio math from the same data as the P–T Slider, right here, no internet needed. If Frosty doesn't know, he'll tell you straight and point you at the lesson that covers it.

Frosty is a training helper, not an emergency service. If you've got a real release happening, work your plant's emergency plan first — then come ask why it happened.

The Ammonia Files on YouTube

Saturation values were computed at build time from the CoolProp thermodynamic property library (Bell et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2014) — the same class of published property models the big apps use — and are interpolated between chart points in the app. 93 refrigerants are included; a few blends whose mixture models don't exist in published property data (e.g. R-438A/MO99) are deliberately left out rather than filled in with guessed numbers. Blend values show bubble and dew points where the refrigerant has temperature glide. Always verify against the refrigerant manufacturer's chart and the equipment nameplate before charging, setting controls, or making safety decisions. GWP values are 100-year AR4/AR5 figures commonly published for each refrigerant.
